analysis.one_liner: Cracks down on sham "citizen petitions" brand-name drugmakers file to delay cheaper generic competitors.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate health committee in October 2025 with 3 senators behind it, and has had no hearing, markup, or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name drug companies file "citizen petitions" with the FDA to stall approval of cheaper generic and biosimilar versions of their drugs. This bill tightens the rules: it lists factors the FDA can weigh to spot petitions filed mainly to delay, requires petitioners to file their petition before going to court and within 180 days of knowing the facts, and tells courts to throw out lawsuits that skip or dodge those steps. The goal is to get cheaper generic and biosimilar drugs to market sooner.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take brand-name drugs once a generic or biosimilar becomes available, since delayed competition keeps prices high — generic versions typically cost far less than the brand. The FDA benefits from clearer criteria for fast-tracking petitions that appear to be filed for delay. Generic and biosimilar manufacturers gain quicker approvals of their products.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients paying high brand-name drug prices

how_it_helps.text: The bill lists specific factors the FDA may use to decide whether a citizen petition was filed with the 'primary purpose of delaying' a generic or biosimilar application — including serial petitions, petitions filed just before an approval date, and petitions demanding testing or labeling standards more onerous than those applied to the brand drug itself.

It requires anyone planning to sue the FDA over a drug approval to first file a citizen petition, and to file it within 180 days of learning the facts; courts must dismiss without prejudice lawsuits that skip the petition, dismiss with prejudice lawsuits filed too late, and dismiss suits filed before the FDA has issued a final decision.
It deletes an existing exception and narrows others in the law, closing workarounds that petitioners currently use to avoid the delay-abuse rules.

The practical effect, by design, is that generic and biosimilar applications reach approval sooner instead of being stalled by filings the bill's title calls untimely — which matters because generics typically sell for far less than the brand-name drug they copy.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies pay, in the form of revenue they currently protect by delaying generic and biosimilar competition through petitions and follow-on litigation. Patients who want the FDA to adopt stricter safety standards could also pay, if legitimate safety petitions get caught in the new deadlines and dismissal rules.

drawbacks.text: Citizen petitions are not always sham filings — some raise genuine safety or manufacturing concerns. The bill's mandatory 180-day filing window and its requirement that courts dismiss late-filed suits 'with prejudice' (permanently, not just for now) could leave legitimate, newly discovered safety claims without a forum.

The bill tells courts to dismiss lawsuits over approval issues filed before the FDA issues a final decision on the petition, which delays judicial review of agency decisions that petitioners believe are wrong.

The FDA gains discretion to weigh factors like a petitioner's history of filing delay petitions, which could discourage a company from filing even a well-founded petition if it has filed dubious ones before.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — faster generic and biosimilar competition, and lower drug prices for patients — is substantial and directly targets a delay tactic that brand manufacturers use repeatedly. The cost is real but narrower: some legitimate safety petitions and lawsuits will face tighter deadlines and fewer procedural second chances. On balance the trade favors patients, though the hard dismissal rules for late filings are the part an honest supporter should acknowledge could block a genuine safety claim raised too late.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has sat with no hearing or vote so far.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen introduced the bill on October 16, 2025, joined by Sen. Susan Collins and one other cosponsor from each party — a small, bipartisan group of three senators.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action has been taken: no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no movement out of committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, brand-name drug makers are better off: the bill has not advanced, so the petition-and-litigation delay tactics it targets remain fully available to them.

for.name: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its Senate push.

for.name: Sen. Susan Collins
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it Republican support.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total support to three senators.

against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill since its October 2025 referral.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.role: Industry with a stake in the outcome
against.what_they_did: Citizen petitions are a widely documented tool brand manufacturers use to delay generic and biosimilar competitors; the industry has a direct financial stake in keeping the tactic available.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's three sponsors include two Democrats and one Republican, though no committee action or vote has occurred to show broader support.

industries.note: Brand manufacturers use citizen petitions and follow-on lawsuits to stall approval of generic and biosimilar versions of their drugs, extending the period when they charge brand prices. The bill lists factors for spotting delay-motivated petitions, imposes deadlines, and tells courts to dismiss suits that bypass the process, cutting into that delay strategy.
Their applications would face fewer delay petitions and fewer lawsuits aimed at blocking approval, so their products reach the market sooner and they capture sales from the brand-name version.

industries.industry: Petition-and-litigation consultants and law firms serving brand manufacturers
industries.note: A practice built around serial petitions and filings timed to known approval dates loses its business model when the FDA can flag serial filings and courts must dismiss suits filed before the agency's final decision.

analysis.trajectory: Congress is still in session, but the pattern for a bill like this is unpromising: with only three cosponsors and no committee hearing scheduled, it will likely sit in HELP unless its provisions get attached to a larger FDA user-fee or drug-pricing package, which is how similar citizen-petition reforms have historically tried to reach the floor.
